questions.q: What does a negative test prove, as distinct from a positive test?
options: That the code runs faster than expected
That the code correctly rejects invalid input or blocks a business rule violation
That the code achieves 100% coverage on its own
That the record was successfully rolled back after the test
questions.explain: A positive test proves the happy path works with valid input; a negative test proves the code correctly rejects or errors on invalid input, missing data, or a rule violation.

questions.q: Why is negative-path testing described as especially important on Salesforce specifically?
options: Because a large amount of Salesforce business logic lives in validation rules, required fields, and addError() calls meant to reject bad data
Because Salesforce does not support try/catch blocks
Because negative tests run with different governor limits than positive tests
Because Salesforce automatically deletes any class without negative tests
questions.explain: Validation rules, required fields, and addError() calls all exist specifically to reject invalid data — if a test never exercises that rejection path, nothing actually proves it still works after a future change.

questions.q: In a negative test using try/catch around code that is expected to throw, what should happen in the try block right after the call, if no exception was thrown?
options: Nothing — the test should simply end without comment
The catch block should run anyway
Assert.fail() should be called to force a failure, since the expected exception never occurred
The test should automatically pass
questions.explain: Calling Assert.fail() in the try block (right after the call expected to throw) forces the test to fail if the exception never actually occurred — otherwise a test that silently never throws would pass for the wrong reason.

questions.q: A team writes only positive tests for a method that enforces 'Amount must be greater than zero to close Won.' Months later, a refactor accidentally removes that check. What happens to the existing positive tests?
options: They automatically fail because the business rule was removed
Salesforce blocks the deployment automatically regardless of tests
Code coverage drops to 0% immediately
They keep passing, because none of them ever exercised the invalid/zero-amount case
questions.explain: Without a negative test for the zero-amount case, the existing positive tests have nothing to say about that broken rule — they only ever exercised valid input, so they keep passing even after the rejection logic is gone.

questions.q: What is the purpose of enumerating a method's input space in a table before writing tests?
options: It replaces the need for any assertions
It turns 'did I think of everything' into an explicit checklist of cases to cover with positive and negative tests
It is required by the Apex compiler before deployment
It automatically generates the test class code
questions.explain: Listing out the distinct categories of input (valid, null, invalid, boundary values) ahead of time makes it a concrete checklist rather than a vague sense of having tested 'enough'.
